edges.cite: Preschern, 'Fluent C', resource/ownership patterns

edges.cite: Nygard, 'Release It!', Bulkhead pattern
edges.note: Bulkhead partitions resource pools (thread/connection pools) into isolated compartments per client or function.

edges.cite: Nygard, 'Release It!', stability patterns

edges.cite: Weir & Noble, 'Small Memory Software', Captain Oates
edges.note: Caches are the discretionary memory less-vital components voluntarily sacrifice under pressure so vital tasks proceed.

edges.cite: Weir & Noble, 'Small Memory Software', Captain Oates / Memory Limit

edges.cite: Jones et al., 'The Garbage Collection Handbook', compacting collectors

edges.cite: ZGC / Shenandoah concurrent compaction design

edges.cite: Weir & Noble, 'Small Memory Software', Copy-on-Write

edges.cite: Coplien, 'Advanced C++', Counted Body / COW string

edges.cite: Weir & Noble, 'Small Memory Software', Secondary Storage patterns

edges.cite: Weir & Noble, 'Small Memory Software', Pooled/Fixed Allocation

edges.cite: Weir & Noble, 'Small Memory Software', Fixed vs Variable Allocation
edges.note: Allocate only worst-case fixed sizes (no fragmentation, wasteful) vs allocate exact variable sizes on demand (fragments).

Both relieve explicit frees; lazy cleanup simply never frees whole-run data, letting the OS reclaim at process exit.
RAII releases deterministically at scope exit; lazy cleanup deliberately declines to release lifetime-of-program memory.
Both suit data living for the whole run: allocate once (or never free) and avoid any runtime deallocation machinery.

edges.cite: Kircher & Jain, POSA3, Resource Release patterns
edges.note: Two release triggers: a lease auto-expires after a fixed time vs an evictor releases the least-valuable resource on demand.

edges.cite: Kircher & Jain, POSA3, Leasing

edges.cite: Kleppmann, 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications', ch.8 leases/fencing

edges.cite: Kircher & Jain, POSA3, Resource Lifecycle Manager / Lookup

edges.cite: Kircher & Jain, POSA3, Resource Acquisition patterns

edges.cite: Jones et al., 'The Garbage Collection Handbook', weak references
edges.note: A weak reference is a GC-supported reference that does not keep its target alive and is cleared when the target is collected.

edges.cite: Kircher & Jain, POSA3, Leasing/Pooling
edges.note: Pooled resources are handed out under leases; the pool reclaims a resource when its lease expires and is not renewed.

edges.cite: Coplien Counted Pointer; C++ shared_ptr
edges.note: A shared smart pointer manages the pointee's lifetime by reference counting, deleting it when the last handle drops.
